materials.title: An introduction to machine learning
materials.sourceText:
Machine learning is a way of finding patterns in examples. Instead of writing every rule by hand, we use data to train a model. A model is a mathematical system that uses these patterns to make a prediction about a new example.

In supervised learning, each training example includes an input and a known answer called a label. For example, an email can be paired with the label "spam" or "not spam". The model learns from these labelled examples. Classification means predicting a category, while regression means predicting a numerical value.

Training data is used to fit the model. Test data is kept separate and used to evaluate how well the model works on examples it did not train on. If the model memorizes the training examples but performs poorly on new ones, this is called overfitting.

Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct. It can be misleading when categories are very uneven. If 950 of 1,000 emails are not spam, a model that always predicts "not spam" achieves 95% accuracy, even though it finds none of the spam. We need to choose evaluation measures that match the problem.

materials.title: Precision, recall, and the confusion matrix
materials.sourceText:
Precision is the fraction of positive predictions that are actually correct. Recall is the fraction of real positive cases that the model finds. A spam filter can raise precision by flagging only the most obvious spam, but then it misses more spam and recall falls.

A confusion matrix counts true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives. Accuracy hides this trade-off when one category is much more common than the other. Choose the measure that matches the cost of each kind of mistake.

Precision and recall

Precision: of the messages flagged as spam, how many really are spam?

Recall: of all the real spam, how many did the model find?

A confusion matrix

True positive: spam correctly flagged.
False positive: a wanted message flagged as spam.
False negative: spam that was missed.
True negative: a wanted message left alone.

materials.title: A short recording on overfitting
materials.sourceText:
Overfitting shows up when a model is very accurate on the examples it trained on and much less accurate on new examples. The recording walks through one fix: keep a separate test set and do not use it to choose the model.

Another fix is to prefer a simpler model when two models perform similarly. A simpler model has fewer chances to memorize accidental details in the training examples.

Overfitting shows up when a model is very accurate on the examples it trained on and much less accurate on new examples. The recording walks through one fix: keep a separate test set and do not use it to choose the model.

Another fix is to prefer a simpler model when two models perform similarly. A simpler model has fewer chances to memorize accidental details in the training examples.

materials.title: Encoding, storage, and retrieval
materials.sourceText:
Encoding is the process of turning an experience into a memory that can be stored. Storage keeps that memory over time. Retrieval brings it back when you need it.

A retrieval cue is a piece of information that helps you reach a stored memory. The same experience can be easy or hard to remember depending on the cue. Studying in conditions similar to the exam can make a useful cue more available.

materials.title: Selective and divided attention
materials.sourceText:
Selective attention is the ability to focus on one stream of information and ignore others. In a noisy room, you can follow one conversation and barely notice the rest.

Divided attention means trying to follow more than one demanding task at the same time. Performance usually drops because the tasks compete for the same limited processing. Switching between tasks also has a cost, even when the switch feels instant.

sections.title: One stream at a time
sections.text: Selective attention keeps one stream of information in focus and leaves other streams in the background. A conversation in a noisy room is the example used in the notes.

sections.title: The cost of doing two things
sections.text: Divided attention asks the same limited processing to follow more than one demanding task. Switching between tasks has a cost even when the switch feels instant.

materials.title: Paragraphs with one main point
materials.sourceText:
A paragraph usually develops one main point. The topic sentence states that point. The following sentences explain it, give a reason, or offer an example from the source you are discussing.

Unity means every sentence belongs to that point. If a sentence starts a new point, it belongs in a new paragraph. Coherence means the sentences follow one another in an order the reader can track.

materials.title: Citing ideas from other sources
materials.sourceText:
Why cite

A citation tells the reader which idea came from which source.

What to cite

Cite a fact, argument, or distinctive phrase you took from someone else.
A common fact that every source agrees on usually does not need a citation.

In the text

Name the author and give the reader enough detail to find the source in your reference list.
